questiontext.text: In the Slice Dicing Explorer, the dice of a fault is best described as:

answer.text: The statements in the backward slice of the incorrect variable that are in no slice of a correct variable

feedback.text: Correct — the dice is the failing (incorrect) slice with every correct variable's slice subtracted out.

answer.text: Every statement the program executes on the failing input

feedback.text: That is the whole trace, not the dice; dicing subtracts the correct variables' slices.

answer.text: The union of the slices of all output variables

feedback.text: Dicing subtracts (set-differences) the correct slices; it does not union them.

answer.text: The set of statements common to every output's slice

feedback.text: Those common statements are exactly what dicing removes, not what it keeps.

generalfeedback.text: The dice = slice(incorrect variable) minus the slices of the observed-correct variables. What remains are statements uniquely implicated in the wrong result.

questiontext.text: How does dicing differ from computing a single slice?

answer.text: Slicing computes one slice; dicing set-differences slices — it subtracts correct variables' slices from the incorrect variable's slice

feedback.text: Correct — dicing is a set operation over several slices to narrow the suspect region.

answer.text: They are identical; dicing is just another name for a backward slice

feedback.text: No — dicing combines several slices by subtraction; a slice is a single set.

answer.text: Slicing needs a failing test but dicing does not

feedback.text: Dicing needs an observed-incorrect variable (a failure); a slice alone needs only a criterion.

answer.text: Dicing ignores dependences and just counts executed lines

feedback.text: Dicing starts from real backward slices (dependence-based) and then subtracts.

generalfeedback.text: A slice answers "what can affect v here?" Dicing takes the incorrect variable's slice and removes the slices of variables observed correct, leaving the statements most likely responsible for the bug.

questiontext.text: In the static Summary Stats scenario, which output variable is the one observed to be incorrect (the wrong output)?

answer.text: highest

feedback.text: Correct — the app seeds highest as the wrong output; its slice starts the dice.

answer.text: total

feedback.text: total is observed correct in this scenario, so its slice is subtracted.

answer.text: mean

feedback.text: mean is observed correct here, so its slice is subtracted.

answer.text: nums

feedback.text: nums is the input array, not one of the three returned output variables.

generalfeedback.text: Summary Stats returns total, mean, and highest. The wrong output is highest; total and mean are correct, so the dice = slice(highest) minus slice(total) minus slice(mean).

questiontext.text: In the static Summary Stats scenario, which output variables are observed correct (their slices get subtracted)?

answer.text: total and mean

feedback.text: Correct — only highest is wrong; total and mean are correct, so their slices are subtracted.

answer.text: highest and mean

feedback.text: highest is the incorrect variable, not a correct one.

answer.text: highest and total

feedback.text: highest is the incorrect variable; the correct pair is total and mean.

answer.text: only total

feedback.text: mean is also correct and its slice is subtracted too.

generalfeedback.text: The dice subtracts the slices of every variable observed correct. Here that is total and mean, leaving what is unique to highest.

questiontext.text: Why does dicing subtract the slices of the variables observed correct?

answer.text: A statement that also computes a correct output is unlikely to be the fault, so removing it narrows the suspects

feedback.text: Correct — statements shared with a correct result are largely exonerated, shrinking the search.

answer.text: To make the dice larger so more statements are inspected

feedback.text: Subtraction shrinks the set; the goal is a smaller, more focused suspect region.

answer.text: Because correct variables never share statements with the wrong one

feedback.text: They often do share statements — that sharing is exactly what subtraction removes.

answer.text: To convert the backward slice into a forward slice

feedback.text: Dicing does not change slice direction; it set-differences backward slices.

generalfeedback.text: If a statement helped produce a value that came out correct, it is a weaker suspect for the bug. Subtracting the correct slices leaves statements implicated only in the wrong output.

questiontext.text: Computing the dice from the failing slice and the correct slices is which set operation?

answer.text: Set difference — the failing slice minus the correct slices

feedback.text: Correct — dice = failingSlice with every statement of any correct slice deleted.

answer.text: Set intersection of all the slices

feedback.text: Intersection would keep shared statements; dicing removes them.

answer.text: Set union of all the slices

feedback.text: Union grows the set; dicing subtracts to shrink it.

answer.text: Symmetric difference of the first two slices only

feedback.text: Dicing subtracts every correct slice from the one failing slice, not a symmetric difference of two.

generalfeedback.text: programDice(failing, passing[]) copies the failing slice and deletes every statement found in any passing/correct slice — a set difference.

name.text: Dice is a subset of the failing slice

questiontext.text: The dice is always a subset of the backward slice of the incorrect variable.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — dicing only ever deletes statements from the failing slice, so the dice cannot contain anything outside it.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Subtraction can only remove statements, never add new ones, so the dice stays within the failing slice.

generalfeedback.text: The dice starts as a copy of the failing (incorrect variable's) slice and only has statements removed, so dice is a subset of that slice.

questiontext.text: In the static Summary Stats scenario with the wrong output set to highest, how many statements does the dice contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the dice is s3, s6, s7 and the return of highest: four statements.
7 is the size of the full backward slice of highest before the correct slices are subtracted.
2 is the dynamic dice of the Fare scenario, not this one.
10 is the total number of statements in the program, not the dice.

generalfeedback.text: slice(highest) has 7 statements; subtracting slice(total) and slice(mean) removes s2, s4, s5, leaving 4: s3, s6, s7, return highest.

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, the seeded bug is at s7 highest = total (it assigns total instead of n). Is s7 in the dice?

answer.text: Yes — s7 is in the dice, so the app reports "Bug caught"

feedback.text: Correct — s7 is in slice(highest) but not in slice(total) or slice(mean), so it survives into the dice.

answer.text: No — s7 is subtracted away by the correct slices

feedback.text: s7 does not appear in the total or mean slices, so it is not subtracted; it stays in the dice.

answer.text: Only if you also mark total as incorrect

feedback.text: s7 is already in the dice with just highest wrong; no extra marking is needed.

answer.text: s7 is not in any slice at all

feedback.text: s7 defines highest, so it is in the backward slice of highest.

generalfeedback.text: The bug s7 (highest = total) influences highest but neither total nor mean, so it stays in the dice; the detail panel confirms "Bug caught".

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator scenario, which run is the failing one?

answer.text: age=30, peak=true — expected 12, actual 14

feedback.text: Correct — the adult-peak run is the only one marked fail.

answer.text: age=30, peak=false — expected 10, actual 10

feedback.text: That run passes (10 = 10), so its slice is subtracted.

answer.text: age=12, peak=false — expected 5, actual 5

feedback.text: That run passes, so its slice is subtracted.

answer.text: age=70, peak=false — expected 3, actual 3

feedback.text: That run passes, so its slice is subtracted.

generalfeedback.text: Only age=30, peak=true fails (expected 12, actual 14). Its dynamic slice is the failing slice; the three passing runs' slices are subtracted.

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator scenario, how many statements does the dice contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the dice is s8 and s9: two statements.
4 is the size of the failing run's dynamic slice before subtraction.
0 would be the STATIC dice here; the dynamic dice is 2.
6 is the size of the union of the passing slices, not the dice.

generalfeedback.text: The failing dynamic slice is {s2, s8, s9, s11}; subtracting the passing runs' slices removes s2 and s11, leaving the dice {s8, s9}.

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator scenario, which statements make up the dice?

answer.text: s8 if (peak) and s9 price = price + 2 + 2

feedback.text: Correct — these two survive subtraction of the passing slices.

answer.text: s2 price = 10 and s11 return price

feedback.text: Both appear in passing runs' slices, so both are subtracted out.

answer.text: s4 price = 5 and s6 price = 3

feedback.text: These run only on passing inputs; they are not even in the failing slice.

answer.text: s3 if (age < 18) and s5 else if (age >= 65)

feedback.text: These are in passing slices and not in the failing slice, so not in the dice.

generalfeedback.text: The dice is {s8, s9}: the peak branch and the buggy fare adjustment that only the failing run exercises.

questiontext.text: In dicing, what role does the incorrect variable play?

answer.text: Its backward slice is the starting (failing) set from which the correct slices are subtracted

feedback.text: Correct — the incorrect variable seeds the failing slice that becomes the dice after subtraction.

answer.text: Its slice is subtracted from the others

feedback.text: Reversed — the correct variables' slices are subtracted from the incorrect variable's slice.

answer.text: It is ignored; only correct variables matter

feedback.text: The incorrect variable is essential — it defines the failing slice.

answer.text: It determines the forward slice used as the dice

feedback.text: Dicing uses the backward slice of the incorrect variable, not a forward slice.

generalfeedback.text: The incorrect variable's backward slice is the failing slice; dicing subtracts the correct variables' slices from it to obtain the dice.

name.text: Bug in dice means fault narrowed

questiontext.text: If the faulty statement lies within the computed dice, dicing has narrowed the suspects down to a set that still contains the fault.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — that is the "Bug caught" case: the dice is smaller than the failing slice yet still holds the fault.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: When the fault is in the dice, the search has been narrowed while retaining the fault — the ideal dicing outcome.

generalfeedback.text: A useful dice is small and still contains the fault. Both example scenarios achieve this (s7 in Summary Stats, s9 in Fare), which the app labels "Bug caught".

questiontext.text: What does a smaller dice give the debugger?

answer.text: Fewer statements to inspect while localizing the fault

feedback.text: Correct — a smaller suspect set means less code to examine.

answer.text: A guarantee that the program has no other bugs

feedback.text: Dicing localizes one observed failure; it says nothing about other bugs.

answer.text: Higher statement coverage

feedback.text: Dicing is about fault localization, not coverage.

answer.text: A proof that the correct outputs are truly correct

feedback.text: Correctness of those outputs is an assumption of dicing, not a result of it.

generalfeedback.text: The value of dicing is a narrower region: a smaller dice means the developer inspects fewer candidate statements to find the fault.

questiontext.text:
In Summary Stats:

  • slice(highest) = { s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7, return‑highest }
  • slice(total) = { s2, s4, s5, return‑total }
  • slice(mean) = { s2, s4, s5, s10, return‑mean }

What is the dice = slice(highest) − slice(total) − slice(mean)?

answer.text: { s3, s6, s7, return-highest }

feedback.text: Correct — subtracting s2, s4, s5 (shared with the correct slices) leaves s3, s6, s7 and the return of highest.
Those are exactly the statements REMOVED; they belong to the correct slices.

answer.text: { s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7, return-highest }

feedback.text: That is slice(highest) before any subtraction.
Only the bug remains here, but dicing also keeps s3, s6, and return-highest, which are absent from the correct slices.

generalfeedback.text: s2, s4, s5 appear in slice(total) and slice(mean), so they are subtracted. The dice is { s3, s6, s7, return-highest } — four statements.

name.text: Why s5 is not in the dice

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, why is s5 total = total + n NOT in the dice, even though it is in slice(highest)?

answer.text: Because s5 also appears in the slices of the correct outputs total and mean, so it is subtracted

feedback.text: Correct — s5 helps compute correct outputs too, so dicing removes it.

answer.text: Because s5 is never executed on the failing input

feedback.text: s5 is in slice(highest), so it is part of the failing computation; it is removed by subtraction, not by non-execution.

answer.text: Because s5 has no data dependence on highest

feedback.text: s5 feeds highest via s7; it is in the failing slice. It is removed because it is also in the correct slices.

answer.text: Because s5 is a control statement

feedback.text: s5 is an assignment, not a control node; it is subtracted because it is shared with the correct slices.

generalfeedback.text: total = total + n contributes to total and mean (both correct) as well as highest, so it is in the subtracted slices and drops out of the dice.

name.text: Why s7 is in the dice

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, why IS s7 highest = total in the dice?

answer.text: It is in slice(highest) but in neither slice(total) nor slice(mean), so nothing subtracts it

feedback.text: Correct — s7 influences only highest, so it survives the subtraction.

answer.text: It is in all three slices

feedback.text: If it were in the correct slices it would be subtracted; s7 affects only highest.

answer.text: It is the criterion statement, which is never removed

feedback.text: The criterion is return highest; s7 is a separate assignment kept because it is unique to highest.

answer.text: Because it is executed most often

feedback.text: Dicing is about set membership across slices, not execution frequency.

generalfeedback.text: total and mean do not depend on highest, so s7 (highest = total) is absent from their slices and remains in the dice.

name.text: Why s3 stays in the dice

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, s3 highest = nums[0] is in the dice. What makes it a suspect there?

answer.text: It defines highest and is not in the correct outputs' slices, so it is not subtracted

feedback.text: Correct — s3 influences highest only, so it survives into the dice.

answer.text: It is the seeded bug

feedback.text: The seeded bug is s7; s3 is a suspect kept because it is unique to highest.

answer.text: It appears in slice(mean)

feedback.text: If it were in slice(mean) it would be subtracted; it is not.

answer.text: It reads total

feedback.text: s3 reads nums, not total; it is kept because it defines highest and is absent from the correct slices.

generalfeedback.text: Dicing keeps every failing-slice statement absent from the correct slices — including s3, an initializer of highest. The dice is a set of suspects, not a single line.

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, why is s2 total = 0 removed from the dice?

answer.text: It is in slice(total) and slice(mean), so both correct slices subtract it

feedback.text: Correct — s2 initializes total, which feeds the correct outputs, so it is removed.

answer.text: It is not in slice(highest)

feedback.text: s2 IS in slice(highest) via total to s7; it is removed by subtraction, not by absence.

answer.text: It never executes

feedback.text: s2 executes on every run; it is subtracted because it is shared with correct slices.

answer.text: It has no defs

feedback.text: s2 defines total; that is exactly why it appears in the correct slices and gets subtracted.

generalfeedback.text: total = 0 contributes to total and mean (both correct), so it is in the subtracted slices and drops out of the dice.

questiontext.text:
In the dynamic Fare Calculator:

  • failing slice = { s2, s8, s9, s11 }
  • union of passing slices = { s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s11 }

What is the dice = failing − union(passing)?

feedback.text: Correct — subtracting s2 and s11 (shared with passing runs) leaves s8 and s9.
Those are exactly the statements removed, not the ones kept.
That is the failing slice before subtraction.

answer.text: { } (empty)

feedback.text: Empty is the STATIC dice here; the dynamic dice is { s8, s9 }.

generalfeedback.text: s2 and s11 appear in the passing runs' slices and are subtracted, leaving the dice { s8, s9 } — the peak branch and its buggy fare adjustment.

name.text: Why s2 is not in the Fare dice

questiontext.text: In the Fare Calculator, s2 price = 10 is in the failing slice but not in the dice. Why?

answer.text: It also appears in a passing run's slice (e.g. the adult-off run), so it is subtracted

feedback.text: Correct — s2 is shared with passing runs, so dicing removes it.

answer.text: It is not executed on the failing input

feedback.text: s2 runs on every input; it is removed because it is also in passing slices.

answer.text: It is a control statement

feedback.text: s2 is an assignment; it is subtracted because it appears in passing slices.

answer.text: It defines peak

feedback.text: s2 defines price, not peak; it is removed because passing runs' slices contain it.

generalfeedback.text: price = 10 feeds the returned price on passing runs too, so it is in a passing slice and subtracted from the dice.

name.text: Why the criterion s11 is not in the dice

questiontext.text: In the Fare Calculator, why is the criterion statement s11 return price not in the dice, even though it is in every slice?

answer.text: Because it is in every run's slice — including the passing ones — so it is subtracted

feedback.text: Correct — a statement common to passing and failing slices is removed by dicing.

answer.text: Because the criterion statement is excluded by definition

feedback.text: The criterion is included in a slice; here it is removed only because it also appears in passing slices.

answer.text: Because s11 has no dependences

feedback.text: s11 uses price and heads every slice; it is removed by subtraction, not by lacking dependences.

answer.text: Because s11 is the bug

feedback.text: The bug is s9; s11 is removed because it is shared with the passing runs.

generalfeedback.text: return price is in the failing slice and in every passing slice, so it is subtracted — dicing keeps only statements unique to the failing execution.

name.text: Why s8 stays in the Fare dice

questiontext.text: In the Fare Calculator, s8 if (peak) is in the dice although it is not itself the bug. Why does it survive?

answer.text: It is the control parent of s9 in the failing slice, and no passing run's slice contains it

feedback.text: Correct — only the failing run enters the peak branch, so s8 is unique to the failing slice.

answer.text: It appears in every passing slice

feedback.text: If it did, it would be subtracted; the passing runs have peak=false and never make s8 part of their price slice.

answer.text: It defines price

feedback.text: s8 is a control predicate on peak; it controls s9, which defines price.

answer.text: Because the criterion is s8

feedback.text: The criterion is s11 (return price); s8 survives because it is unique to the failing slice.

generalfeedback.text: The failing run takes the peak branch, so s8 controls the buggy s9 and enters the failing slice; the passing runs (peak=false) exclude it, so it is not subtracted. The dice holds suspects, not only the fault.

name.text: Match term to role: passing slice

questiontext.text: In dicing, the slice of a variable/run observed correct serves what role?

answer.text: It is subtracted from the failing slice

feedback.text: Correct — correct slices are the terms removed by set difference.

answer.text: It is the starting set for the dice

feedback.text: The starting set is the failing (incorrect) slice; correct slices are subtracted from it.

answer.text: It is intersected with the failing slice

feedback.text: Dicing subtracts, not intersects, the correct slices.

answer.text: It is ignored

feedback.text: Correct slices are central — they are exactly what narrows the dice.

generalfeedback.text: Failing slice = starting set; correct (passing) slices = subtracted terms; dice = the residual.

name.text: Match term to role: the dice

questiontext.text: In dicing, the dice is:

answer.text: The residual suspect set left after subtracting the correct slices

feedback.text: Correct — the dice is what remains of the failing slice after subtraction.

answer.text: The union of all output slices

feedback.text: That is not the dice; dicing subtracts, and the dice is the residual.

answer.text: The backward slice of a correct variable

feedback.text: A correct variable's slice is a subtracted term, not the dice.

answer.text: The full trace of the failing run

feedback.text: The trace is not the dice; the dice is a subset of the failing slice.

generalfeedback.text: The dice is the residual: failing slice minus the correct slices, i.e. the statements most likely to hold the fault.

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, starting from slice(highest) = { s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7, return-highest }, which statements does subtracting slice(total) = { s2, s4, s5, return-total } remove?

feedback.text: Correct — those three are the members shared between slice(highest) and slice(total).

answer.text: s2, s4, s5, return-total

feedback.text: return-total is not in slice(highest), so it cannot be removed from it.
Those are NOT in slice(total), so they are not removed by this subtraction.

answer.text: nothing

feedback.text: slice(highest) and slice(total) share s2, s4, s5, which are removed.

generalfeedback.text: Set difference removes only the shared members: slice(highest) ∩ slice(total) = { s2, s4, s5 }. (slice(mean) later removes nothing new.)

name.text: Statement not even in the failing slice

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, is s10 mean = total / nums.length in the dice for the wrong output highest?

answer.text: No — s10 is not even in slice(highest), so it is never a candidate for the dice

feedback.text: Correct — highest does not depend on mean, so s10 is absent from the failing slice and thus from the dice.

answer.text: Yes — s10 is in the dice

feedback.text: s10 computes mean, on which highest does not depend, so it is not in slice(highest) or the dice.

answer.text: No — but only because slice(mean) subtracts it

feedback.text: s10 is not in slice(highest) to begin with, so there is nothing to subtract; it is absent regardless.

answer.text: Only if mean is also wrong

feedback.text: Even then s10 is not in slice(highest); the dice is a subset of slice(highest).

generalfeedback.text: The dice is a subset of the failing slice. Because highest does not depend on mean, s10 is outside slice(highest) and can never be in the highest-dice — a different reason from being subtracted.

name.text: Multiple passing runs are all subtracted

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator, dicing subtracts the union of the slices of all three passing runs from the failing run's slice.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — every passing run's slice is removed, i.e. their union is subtracted from the failing slice.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: programDice deletes each passing slice in turn, which is the same as subtracting their union.

generalfeedback.text: Deleting the members of each passing slice one after another is equivalent to subtracting the union of all passing slices from the failing slice.

name.text: Statement in both failing and a passing slice

questiontext.text: A statement is in the failing slice AND in at least one passing/correct slice. Is it in the dice?

answer.text: No — appearing in any correct/passing slice removes it from the dice

feedback.text: Correct — set difference deletes it because it is shared with a correct slice.

answer.text: Yes — being in the failing slice is enough

feedback.text: Being in a correct slice as well causes it to be subtracted out.

answer.text: Only if it is a control statement

feedback.text: Kind does not matter; any statement shared with a correct slice is removed.

answer.text: Only if it is the criterion

feedback.text: Even the criterion is removed if it is in a passing slice, as s11 shows in the Fare scenario.

generalfeedback.text: The dice keeps only statements in the failing slice AND in NO correct slice. Sharing with any correct slice excludes a statement.

name.text: Why the bug is isolated (Summary Stats)

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, which chain of reasoning explains why the bug s7 highest = total lands in the dice?

answer.text: s7 is in slice(highest) because highest transitively depends on it; and s7 is absent from slice(total) and slice(mean) because neither total nor mean depends on highest, so nothing subtracts it

feedback.text: Correct — present in the failing slice, absent from the correct slices, therefore in the dice.

answer.text: s7 executes only on the failing input, so it is added to the dice

feedback.text: This is the static scenario; s7 executes on all inputs. It is kept by set membership, not by execution.

answer.text: s7 is in all three slices but is kept because it is the bug

feedback.text: Dicing does not know which statement is the bug; s7 survives because it is not in the correct slices.

answer.text: s7 is the criterion, which is never subtracted

feedback.text: The criterion is return highest; s7 is a distinct statement kept by the set-difference logic.

generalfeedback.text: Dicing is purely set membership: s7 influences highest (in the failing slice) but not total or mean (not in the correct slices), so it survives into the dice. The app then reports "Bug caught".

name.text: When the fault is guaranteed to be in the dice

questiontext.text: Dicing puts the fault in the dice only if which assumption holds?

answer.text: The variables/runs marked correct really are correct (their slices are fault-free) and the fault does affect the incorrect variable

feedback.text: Correct — if a "correct" slice actually contains the fault, subtraction removes the fault from the dice.

answer.text: The program has 100% statement coverage

feedback.text: Coverage is unrelated; dicing depends on which variables are correct/incorrect.

answer.text: The failing slice is empty

feedback.text: An empty failing slice would give an empty dice with no fault at all.

answer.text: Every output is incorrect

feedback.text: Then there would be no correct slice to subtract, and dicing would not narrow anything.

generalfeedback.text: If a variable labeled correct is coincidentally correct despite executing the faulty statement, that statement is in the subtracted slice and is wrongly removed. Dicing's guarantee rests on the correctness labels being accurate.

name.text: When the dice comes out empty

questiontext.text: The app can report "The dice is empty — all outputs share this region of code." When does that happen?

answer.text: When every statement in the failing slice also appears in some correct variable's slice

feedback.text: Correct — then subtraction removes everything and the dice is empty.

answer.text: When the failing slice is larger than every correct slice

feedback.text: Size does not determine emptiness; overlap does. A large failing slice can still leave a non-empty dice.

answer.text: When there is exactly one output variable

feedback.text: With one output there is nothing correct to subtract, so the dice equals the failing slice (not empty).

answer.text: Whenever the bug is found

feedback.text: Finding the bug means it is IN the dice, i.e. the dice is non-empty.

generalfeedback.text: An empty dice means the correct slices cover the whole failing slice — the outputs share that region, so dicing cannot narrow the fault there.

name.text: Why dynamic dicing succeeds where static fails (Fare)

questiontext.text: In the Fare Calculator, the app notes the static dice would be empty but the dynamic dice is { s8, s9 }. Why?

answer.text: Static slices are input-independent, so the failing and passing static slices coincide and the difference is empty; dynamic slices restrict to executed statements and live dependences, distinguishing the failing run

feedback.text: Correct — dynamic slicing separates the failing execution's actual dependences from the passing ones.

answer.text: Static slicing ignores control dependences

feedback.text: Static slicing includes control dependences; the issue is input-independence, not missing control edges.

answer.text: The dynamic dice adds statements not in any slice

feedback.text: The dynamic dice is still a subset of the failing dynamic slice; it adds nothing.

answer.text: Dynamic dicing subtracts fewer slices

feedback.text: It subtracts the same three passing runs; what differs is that dynamic slices are execution-specific.

generalfeedback.text: Statically, every path's slice of price looks the same, so failing minus passing is empty. Dynamically, only the failing run's slice contains s8 and s9 (the peak branch and its buggy update), so the dynamic dice isolates them.

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator, the failing slice is { s2, s8, s9, s11 }. The passing dynamic slices are: adult-off = { s2, s11 }, child-off = { s3, s4, s11 }, senior-off = { s3, s5, s6, s11 }. Which passing run's slice is what removes s2 from the dice?

answer.text: The adult-off run (age=30, peak=false), whose slice contains s2

feedback.text: Correct — only adult-off's slice includes s2, so it is what subtracts it.

answer.text: The child-off run

feedback.text: child-off's slice is { s3, s4, s11 } — it does not contain s2.

answer.text: The senior-off run

feedback.text: senior-off's slice is { s3, s5, s6, s11 } — it does not contain s2.

answer.text: No passing run removes s2; it stays in the dice

feedback.text: adult-off's slice contains s2, so s2 is subtracted and is not in the dice.

generalfeedback.text: Only adult-off's dynamic slice includes s2 (its returned price traces back to price = 10). That membership subtracts s2, leaving the dice { s8, s9 }.

name.text: Why the dice narrows fault localization

questiontext.text: Compared with inspecting the failing slice alone, why does the dice narrow fault localization in Summary Stats?

answer.text: The failing slice has 7 statements; the dice has 4, because statements exonerated by the correct outputs are removed

feedback.text: Correct — subtracting the correct slices shrinks 7 suspects to 4.

answer.text: The dice adds statements the failing slice missed

feedback.text: The dice is a subset of the failing slice; it never adds statements.

answer.text: The dice re-orders the statements by suspicion but keeps all 7

feedback.text: Dicing removes statements; it does not merely re-order them.

answer.text: The dice guarantees exactly one statement remains

feedback.text: Here 4 remain; dicing narrows but rarely to a single line.

generalfeedback.text: Dicing removes s2, s4, s5 (shared with the correct total and mean), cutting the suspect set from 7 to 4 while still containing the bug s7.

name.text: When a fault lies outside the dice

questiontext.text: A faulty statement can end up OUTSIDE the dice. How?

answer.text: If the faulty statement also belongs to a correct variable's slice, it is subtracted and the dice misses it

feedback.text: Correct — shared faults are exonerated by the subtraction, a known limitation of dicing.

answer.text: If the faulty statement is in the failing slice

feedback.text: Being in the failing slice is what keeps it a candidate, not what excludes it.

answer.text: Dicing can never miss the fault

feedback.text: It can: if the fault is shared with a correct slice it is subtracted out.

answer.text: Only if the program has no loops

feedback.text: Loops are irrelevant; the issue is the fault being shared with a correct slice.

generalfeedback.text: If a statement both causes the failure and contributes to a value that happened to be correct, dicing subtracts it and the dice misses the fault. This is why the correctness of the "correct" labels matters.

questiontext.text: In Summary Stats, the detail panel shows "Bug caught (s7: assigns total, not n)". What does this confirm?

answer.text: The seeded bug statement s7 is a member of the computed dice

feedback.text: Correct — "Bug caught" means the bug id is in the dice set.

answer.text: The program is now fixed

feedback.text: Dicing localizes; it does not repair code.

answer.text: The dice contains exactly one statement

feedback.text: The dice here has four statements; s7 is just one of them.

answer.text: total and mean are also wrong

feedback.text: total and mean are the correct outputs; only highest is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: "Bug caught" is displayed when the scenario's bug statement is inside the dice — evidence that dicing retained the fault while narrowing the suspects.

name.text: A suspect that is not the fault

questiontext.text: In the Fare Calculator, s8 if (peak) is in the dice but is not the bug. What does its presence illustrate about dicing?

answer.text: The dice is a set of suspects, not a single line — control/data ancestors unique to the failing run remain, so dicing narrows without pinpointing

feedback.text: Correct — dicing produces a reduced region, still possibly holding non-faulty statements.

answer.text: Dicing made an error; s8 should not be there

feedback.text: s8 is correctly in the dice — it is unique to the failing slice; dicing does not claim every dice member is faulty.

answer.text: s8 must also be buggy

feedback.text: Only s9 is the seeded bug; s8 is a non-faulty suspect kept by the set logic.

answer.text: The dice should be empty

feedback.text: The dynamic dice is { s8, s9 }, correctly non-empty and containing the fault.

generalfeedback.text: s8 controls the buggy s9 and is unique to the failing execution, so it stays. Dicing narrows the search but the dice can include non-faulty statements around the fault.

name.text: Effect of subtracting fewer correct slices

questiontext.text: Suppose in Summary Stats only total is treated as correct (mean is not subtracted). The dice becomes slice(highest) − slice(total). What happens to the dice compared with subtracting both total and mean?

answer.text: The dice can only stay the same or grow — subtracting fewer slices never removes more

feedback.text: Correct — set difference is monotonic; fewer subtractions cannot shrink the dice. (Here it stays { s3, s6, s7, return-highest } because slice(mean) removed nothing new.)

answer.text: The dice can only shrink

feedback.text: Reversed — removing a subtracted slice can only keep or enlarge the dice.

answer.text: The dice becomes empty

feedback.text: Subtracting fewer slices cannot empty a previously non-empty dice.

answer.text: The bug s7 drops out

feedback.text: s7 is not in slice(total), so it stays regardless of whether mean is subtracted.

generalfeedback.text: Each subtracted slice can only remove statements. Dropping slice(mean) can only keep or enlarge the dice. In this example the dice is unchanged, since slice(mean) added no new removals beyond slice(total).

questiontext.text: Adding one more correct-variable slice to subtract can only keep the dice the same or make it smaller — never larger.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — each additional subtracted slice can only delete statements, so the dice is monotonically non-increasing.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Set difference only removes; another subtracted slice cannot add statements back.

generalfeedback.text: dice = failing minus (union of correct slices). Enlarging the subtracted union can only remove more, so more correct slices give a smaller-or-equal dice.

questiontext.text: Why is dicing described as fault localization rather than fault detection?

answer.text: It assumes a failure is already observed (a variable known incorrect) and narrows WHERE the fault is; it does not decide whether an output is wrong

feedback.text: Correct — you must already know which variable is incorrect before dicing can localize it.

answer.text: It generates new failing test inputs

feedback.text: Dicing does not create tests; it works from an observed failure.

answer.text: It proves the absence of bugs

feedback.text: Dicing localizes an observed fault; it proves nothing about absence of bugs.

answer.text: It measures coverage of the failing run

feedback.text: Dicing is not a coverage metric; it computes a suspect set.

generalfeedback.text: Dicing needs the correct/incorrect labels as input — a failure must already be detected. Given that, it localizes the fault to the dice.

name.text: Why s2 is in the failing slice yet dropped (Fare)

questiontext.text: In the dynamic Fare Calculator, explain the status of s2 price = 10: it is in the failing slice but not in the dice.

answer.text: On the failing run, s2's price is the value read at s9 (a live definition), so s2 is in the failing slice; but s2 is also in a passing run's slice, so dicing subtracts it

feedback.text: Correct — in the failing slice by a live data dependence, then removed because it is shared with a passing slice.

answer.text: s2 is not executed on the failing run

feedback.text: s2 runs on every input, including the failing one.

answer.text: s2 is a control statement with no data flow

feedback.text: s2 is an assignment defining price; it has data flow into s9.

answer.text: s2 is the criterion

feedback.text: The criterion is s11 (return price); s2 is an ordinary assignment.

generalfeedback.text: On the failing run price = 10 is the last definition of price reaching s9, so s2 is in the failing dynamic slice. Because adult-off's slice also contains s2, the subtraction removes it from the dice.

questiontext.text: Dicing's result depends on which variables you declare correct vs incorrect. If a genuinely-correct output is mistakenly marked incorrect (or vice versa), what is the consequence?

answer.text: The dice changes and may exclude the true fault or include irrelevant statements — dicing's usefulness hinges on accurate correct/incorrect labels

feedback.text: Correct — the labels choose which slices are subtracted, so mislabeling distorts the dice.

answer.text: Nothing changes; the dice is independent of the labels

feedback.text: The labels determine the failing slice and the subtracted slices, so the dice depends on them.

answer.text: The dice always becomes empty

feedback.text: Not always; mislabeling shifts which statements are subtracted, not necessarily to empty.

answer.text: The program is automatically re-tested

feedback.text: Dicing does not run tests; it recomputes a set from the given labels.

generalfeedback.text: Which variable is incorrect sets the failing slice; which are correct sets the subtracted slices. Wrong labels can subtract the fault away or leave noise in the dice, so accurate labeling is essential.

questiontext.text: Which ordering correctly describes the dicing procedure the app performs?

answer.text: 1) take the incorrect variable and compute its backward slice; 2) compute the slices of the correct variables; 3) subtract the correct slices from the incorrect slice; 4) inspect the remaining dice for the fault

feedback.text: Correct — failing slice first, then subtract the correct slices, then read the dice.

answer.text: 1) union all output slices; 2) intersect with the trace; 3) report the intersection

feedback.text: Dicing subtracts correct slices from the failing slice; it does not union then intersect.

answer.text: 1) compute forward slice of the bug; 2) subtract the failing slice; 3) report

feedback.text: Dicing uses backward slices and starts from the incorrect variable, not a known bug.

answer.text: 1) run all tests; 2) keep statements covered by every test; 3) report them

feedback.text: That describes common coverage, not dicing's set difference of slices.

generalfeedback.text: Dicing: backward-slice the incorrect variable, backward-slice the correct variables, subtract the correct slices from the incorrect slice, and inspect the resulting dice for the fault.
